title: K. v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
summary: In the case of K. v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicants were a family of Serbian nationals of Ashkaelia/Roma origin from Kosovo, represented by lawyers in Skopje. Their case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Ashkaelia minorities facing ethnic violence and insecurity in post-conflict Kosovo, particularly the risk of life-threatening and degrading treatment if forcibly returned. After living in Germany with asylum status from 1993 to 2003, the family was deported to Kosovo, where they encountered severe ethnic unrest and displacement, including the occupation of their home and subsequent violence in March 2004. Fearing for their safety, they fled to the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia in July 2004 and sought asylum, but their request was summarily dismissed, and they were ordered to leave the country. Despite interim measures from the European Court of Human Rights to prevent their expulsion, the family ultimately left Macedonia voluntarily and returned to Kosovo. The Court examined potential violations of Articles 2 (right to life), 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), and 13 (right to an effective remedy), but ultimately struck the case out after the applicants withdrew their complaint. This case underscores the precarious situation of Roma and Ashkaelia minorities in the Balkans during the early 2000s, reflecting broader patterns of displacement and insecurity faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe.
